Overview Icarus & his friends have crafted handmade wings. Day and night, jubilant with their newfound freedom, they fly higher & higher… With competitive (2-5p) and co-operative (3-5p) modes, players win tricks to fly higher in the sky. The winner of each trick moves to the next open space above them on the scoring track unless they fly into the sun, in which case they will plummet to below the bottom-most player. Quick summary In this must-follow trick-taking game, every card has two sides: a Day side and Night side. When it is Day, Yellow is the trump color. When it is Night, White is the trump color. Whenever a number 5-card is played, the active sides of all cards held and on the table are immediately flipped. The winner of each trick will fly up to the next open space on the scoring track. If the trick includes the Lightning Card, the winner of that trick will instead fall down to the next open space below. When a player flies into the sun: They immediately fall down to just below the bottommost player The current round will be the last. Whoever is highest in the sky at the end of the last round wins. Setup Rounds Trickarus is played over a number of rounds, until 1 player flies into the Sun whereupon the game concludes at the end of that round (exception: A 2 player game is always only 1 round). The cards The playing cards have 4 different colours (suits) Yellow (sun) Pink (cloud) Blue (rain) White (moon) Every playing card has a day half and a night half. At the beginning of the game, everyone starts with the cards arranged so that the day half is at the top. Three of the cards are of value 0 and consist of a different suit in each half: Cloud / Rain Sun / Cloud Rain / Moon There is also a single Lightning card in the deck. Dealing cards At the start of a round, the cards are shuffled and dealt. The number of cards selected + dealt is dependent on the number of players: Players Cards removed Number of cards per player 2 4 Sun, 6 Sun, & Lightning card 13 3 0 Cloud / Rain 13 4 None 10 5 None 8 The day marker The day / night marker shows whether it is “Day” or “Night”, and which side of the cards is currently “active”: The Day side has a light background The Night side has a dark background The day marker is placed in view of all players. [Rating: 2/10] Strange one, because it is simultaneously too chaotic and too predictable—an oxymoronic combo. Turn by turn mayhem, but the overall arc is formulaic. You can never know when the flipping 5-cards will come out, but you [i]do[/i] know how many there are (and in which suit), so you can generally expect when a reversal might take place. On the other hand, even when you’ve correctly anticipated it, you can't always plan or protect for it. [Rating: 3/10] Another novelty trick-taker that doesn't live up to the hype. Almost entirely void of meaningful decisions, the small handsize and chaos mean your entire hand is virtually programmed by the deal. Tiresome.

[Rating: 4/10] If I didn't win a hand, I was generally playing the only card I could play to follow suit. The day/night switching is cool, but I never had a choice to trigger it, I had to because the 5 was the only card I had! The flying into the sun is funny but probably frustrating when it happens to you!

[Rating: 4/10] 2025-12-31, 4/10 @ 42 plays:  My feelings have not changed. It still feels very random.  2025-12-11, 4/10 @ 36 plays:  I like the idea, but the gameplay itself has too much randomness and too little player agency. When you win, it does not feel like it was because of any real skill on your part. The fun is mostly in the tension of the final few rounds, when everyone is near the top of the track, but that excitement wore off for me quite quickly.

[Rating: 5/10] A trick taking game where players score points by winning tricks and move up (skipping any players, if any) the game scoring track. If you reach the top of the stack, end game is triggered and you restart back to the bottom. The player highest on the scoring track wins.

[Rating: 5/10] Initial impression: - Works, was fun, leans more on the chaotic side, I can imagine that it gets a bit boring with more plays. But glad to have tried it.

[Rating: 5.5/10] The second and third hands were interesting. Having the middle card be the one that flips cards around and changes trump was a good design choice. But, in a game with only 2-3 hands, the first hand feels really un-impactful and like it was just extended setup for the second hand.

[Rating: 5.5/10] 1 play, 4p: Not sure how I feel about this game after one play. It seems a bit chaotic with the fives reversing cards played. I usually like games with chaos, but this felt more like an activity.   Overall, I would try it again to see if I'm missing something, but there are many better trick-taking games out there.
